newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Optus says wanted PBL deal secret.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Optus says wanted PBL deal secret.

text.p: Optus Communications Pty Ltd said on Tuesday it made a deal with Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL) over the ownership of Optus Vision and it did not want Seven Network Ltd to know about it, as Seven may pass the details onto its shareholder News Corp Ltd.

Optus Communications lawyer Jeff Sher told the Supreme Court of New South Wales that News' knowledge of the deal, known as the PBL agreement, could affect Optus Vision's plans, as News Corp owned 50 percent of Foxtel, a pay TV rival to Optus Vision.
Seven had alleged the PBL agreement would breach the Optus Vision's shareholders agreement.
"This is a highly volatile, competitive industry of which there are three players and only two really matter," Sher told the court.

"At a critical time, there was a change in ownership at Seven and that new shareholder had a substantial relationship with News Ltd (a unit of News Corp), some would say a controlled (relationship)," Sher said.
"There was a Trojan Horse in the camp and the matter had to be kept confidential from the only competition that really mattered," he said.
News Corp has a 15 percent stake in Seven.

Perth-based businessman Kerry Stokes became Seven largest shareholder after a share-buying spree in early-1995 and became chairman of the television network on June 27, 1995. Stokes currently owns about 24 percent of the television network.
Stokes is seen by many market pundits as close to the News Corp camp as he has a business relationship with News Ltd chairman Ken Cowley.

Foxtel and Optus Vision are seen as the main pay TV players, the third, satellite operator Australis Media Ltd is seen as a minor player and nearly collapsed last year before a financial bailout involving PBL came to the rescue.

Under the orginal agreement, PBL had an option to increase its Optus Vision stake from its current five percent by July 1997, at which time it would exit its holding in the Optus Vision sports channel, Sportsvision.

Seven's litigation follows an agreement signed last year between Optus Communications, U.S. West Inc, which both holds 46.5 percent of Optus Vision, and Kerry Packer's media group PBL that allowed PBL to extend the right of its option agreement by six months and keep its Sportsvision stake.
Optus has not entered any deal with Seven that allowed it to extend its option right.

PBL would also have the opportunity to raise its stake to 33 percent under the new agreement if Seven decided not to exercise its own option to raise its Optus Vision stake to 15 percent from two percent.
"The agreement was formed in compliance with the shareholder agreement. If it did not comply it cannot be enforced," Sher told the court.
Seven has said the deal between PBL, Optus Communications and U.S. West followed PBL's part in the Australis rescue.
Australis has also formed a satellite TV joint venture with Optus Vision last year.

"There were enormous benefits by bringing Australis into the Vision camp. Nine selfishly, purposely and legitimately sought to improve its position because its bargainging power had increased," Sher told the court.
Australis also has programming arrangements with Foxtel, which is half owned by Telstra Corp.
If Seven Network wins the case, which is expected to take at least two weeks, it says it would be entitled to buy the remaining 98 percent of Optus Vision it does not already own.
Seven has said it would on-sell Optus Vision to an overseas telephone company.
Seven's court action, through its subsidiary Tallglen Pty Ltd, has delayed the float of Optus Communications, Australia's second biggest communications company.
Optus Communications is 25 percent owned by Mayne Nickless Ltd and 24.5 percent each by BellSouth Corp and Cable and Wireless Plc.
Seven shares closed three cents higher at A$4.34.
-- Kevin Morrison, Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1813
